programs.name: Medi-Cal Medicare Savings Programs (QMB, SLMB, QI)
programs.tagline: California pays your loved one's Medicare premiums and out-of-pocket costs if their income is under $1,796/month

localEntities.name: Local county social services agency (find via county website or DHCS directory)

programs.intro:
If your loved one has Medicare and limited income, California's Medicare Savings Programs can eliminate their monthly Medicare costs entirely. The highest tier (QMB) covers all Medicare Part A and Part B premiums, deductibles, and copays for people earning under $1,330/month. Mid-tier programs (SLMB and QI) cover Part B premiums for those earning up to $1,796/month.

Unlike federal programs, California allows up to $130,000 in assets for singles ($195,000 for couples), so your loved one's home and savings likely won't disqualify them. Because this works like automatic Medigap coverage, your loved one won't get surprise medical bills, providers cannot legally charge QMB recipients for Medicare cost-sharing.

The program is administered county-by-county through local social services agencies. QI funding comes from a limited federal block grant, so it may have waitlists or temporary closures when funds run out.
programs.savingsSource: All three Medicare Savings Programs pay the Medicare Part B premium, which is $202.90 a month in 2026, or about $2,434 a year. QMB also covers Medicare deductibles and copays. Someone already on full-scope Medi-Cal may already have the premium paid, so this is not always additional.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house worth $300,000 and still qualify?
faqs.answer: Yes. California allows up to $130,000 in countable assets for singles ($195,000 for couples), and your primary home doesn't count toward this limit regardless of value. Most personal belongings, one car, and burial plots are also exempt.

faqs.question: What if my loved one is already on regular Medi-Cal?
faqs.answer: They should still apply for Medicare Savings Programs. These programs specifically pay Medicare premiums and cost-sharing that regular Medi-Cal may not cover. You can have both programs simultaneously.

faqs.question: What happens if the QI program runs out of money?
faqs.answer: QI is funded by a limited federal block grant that can be exhausted. If denied due to lack of funds, reapply when the next federal fiscal year begins (October 1st). Consider SLMB as an alternative if your loved one's income qualifies.

faqs.question: Does my loved one need to be enrolled in Medicare Part B before applying?
faqs.answer: Yes, Medicare Part B enrollment is required before you can apply. If your loved one only has Part A, they need to enroll in Part B first through Social Security or Medicare.gov. QMB recipients get automatically enrolled in Part A as of 2025.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can apply as authorized representatives. You'll need to complete additional authorization forms with your county social services office and may need legal documentation depending on your loved one's capacity.

faqs.question: How far back can benefits be applied?
faqs.answer: The QMB program has no retroactive coverage; benefits start the month after you are approved. SLMB and QI currently provide up to 3 months of backdated coverage, but be aware that this will be limited to 2 months starting in 2027.

faqs.question: What if a doctor tries to bill my loved one for Medicare copays?
faqs.answer: Providers cannot legally bill QMB recipients for Medicare deductibles, copays, or coinsurance. If this happens, contact your county Medi-Cal office immediately. To prevent issues, choose providers who accept Medi-Cal patients.

faqs.question: Do these programs affect Medicare Advantage or Medigap plans?
faqs.answer: If your loved one has QMB, they don't need Medigap since all Medicare costs are covered. They can still have Medicare Advantage, and the program will cover any Medicare-approved cost-sharing. SLMB and QI recipients may still benefit from Medigap for costs not covered by Medicare Savings Programs.

programs.name: Multipurpose Senior Services Program Waiver (MSSP)
programs.tagline: If your loved one needs daily care but wants to stay home, this California program provides nursing oversight, personal care, meals, and other services to avoid nursing home placement.

localEntities.name: Local MSSP sites via California Department of Aging (CDA)

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60+ and needs help with daily activities like bathing, dressing, or medication management, California's MSSP Waiver can provide comprehensive home care services to help them avoid nursing home placement. The program combines nursing oversight, personal care assistance, home-delivered meals, adult day care, and transportation, all coordinated by one care team.

Your loved one must already qualify for Medi-Cal and pass a clinical assessment showing they need nursing facility-level care. Because MSSP serves only specific counties and has limited slots (11,940 statewide per year), eligibility doesn't guarantee enrollment. Services are tailored to each person's needs but must cost less than nursing home care to qualify.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for MSSP if they live in any California county?
faqs.answer: No, MSSP is only available in counties that have contracted providers. Counties like Alpine, Colusa, El Dorado, Placer, Sacramento, Sutter, Yolo, Yuba, Los Angeles, and Ventura have providers, but many counties do not. Contact the California Department of Aging at (916) 419-7500 to verify availability in your loved one's county.

faqs.question: What if my loved one meets all requirements but there's a waitlist?
faqs.answer: MSSP is capped at 11,940 slots statewide, so eligible applicants often wait months for enrollment. Ask your local provider about their current waitlist length and whether they offer any crisis prioritization. You can also explore In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) as an alternative while waiting.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get MSSP services if they're already receiving In-Home Supportive Services?
faqs.answer: It depends on the specific services. MSSP cannot duplicate services your loved one is already receiving through other Medi-Cal programs like Enhanced Care Management or Targeted Case Management. The MSSP provider will review all current services and coordinate to avoid duplication.

faqs.question: How much care can MSSP provide compared to a nursing home?
faqs.answer: MSSP can provide extensive services including 24/7 personal care if needed, but the total cost must remain below what nursing home care would cost in your area. If your loved one needs very intensive medical supervision that would exceed nursing home costs, they may not qualify for MSSP.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's Medi-Cal eligibility changes while enrolled in MSSP?
faqs.answer: Your loved one must maintain Medi-Cal eligibility to continue receiving MSSP services. If they lose Medi-Cal eligibility, MSSP services will end. California has eliminated asset limits for most Medi-Cal programs, so participants simply need to keep meeting Medi-Cal eligibility and functional care requirements to stay enrolled.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my loved one who has dementia?
faqs.answer: Yes, family members can initiate the MSSP application process for parents with cognitive impairment. However, the registered nurse assessment must be conducted with your loved one present, and you may need legal documentation like power of attorney to make healthcare decisions on their behalf.

faqs.question: How long can my loved one stay enrolled in MSSP?
faqs.answer: MSSP enrollment continues as long as your loved one remains Medi-Cal eligible, needs nursing facility level of care, and their service costs stay below nursing home rates. The care team conducts regular reassessments to ensure services still meet their needs and program requirements.

faqs.question: What's the difference between MSSP and regular Medi-Cal managed care?
faqs.answer: MSSP provides intensive care coordination and home-based services specifically for people at risk of nursing home placement. Regular Medi-Cal covers medical care but doesn't include the comprehensive personal care, meals, transportation, and 24/7 care management that MSSP offers.

programs.name: Community Based Adult Services (CBAS)
programs.tagline: Daytime health supervision and activities for adults who need help with daily care but live at home.
programs.intro:
If your loved one has dementia, chronic illness, or needs daily help with bathing or medication management, CBAS provides daytime supervision and health services at adult day centers, up to 7 days per week. This Medi-Cal program helps aging adults stay in their own homes instead of moving to nursing facilities, while giving family caregivers respite during the day.

Your loved one must be enrolled in a Medi-Cal Managed Care Plan and meet functional eligibility requirements through a face-to-face assessment with a registered nurse. The program operates in 28 California counties with 310 certified centers, but you must live within one hour's drive of a participating center.

Starting January 1, 2026, new asset limits apply: $130,000 for individuals and $195,000 for couples. Income limits follow standard Medi-Cal thresholds, which vary by household size and are updated annually by the state.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get CBAS if they're not enrolled in a Medi-Cal Managed Care Plan?
faqs.answer: Very limited options exist. Most CBAS participants must be enrolled in a Medi-Cal Managed Care Plan. Los Angeles has a special field office for fee-for-service Medi-Cal beneficiaries exempt from managed care, but this is rare. Your loved one would need to enroll in managed care first in most counties.

faqs.question: What if the nearest CBAS center is more than one hour away?
faqs.answer: Your loved one would not be eligible for CBAS. The program requires residence within one hour's drive of a certified center. Only 28 of California's 58 counties have CBAS centers. You might explore In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) as an alternative.

faqs.question: Will my loved one's house count against the $130,000 asset limit?
faqs.answer: No, the primary residence is exempt from CBAS asset limits. However, other property, bank accounts, and investments do count. The limits are $130,000 for individuals and $195,000 for couples as of January 1, 2026.

faqs.question: Can I apply for CBAS and IHSS at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, these are separate programs that can complement each other. CBAS provides daytime services at centers, while IHSS provides in-home care assistance. Both go through your Medi-Cal Managed Care Plan, which can coordinate applications.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's dementia is only stage 3?
faqs.answer: Stage 3 dementia alone may not qualify, but your loved one might still be eligible under other criteria like needing Nursing Facility Level of Care. The registered nurse assessment using the CEDT tool evaluates functional abilities regardless of dementia stage.

faqs.question: How many days per week can my loved one attend CBAS?
faqs.answer: Members can be approved for services up to 7 days per week depending on their assessed needs and the managed care plan's authorization. The specific schedule depends on your loved one's functional assessment and the center's capacity.

programs.name: CalFresh
programs.tagline: Up to $306/month for groceries (from October 1, 2026) if your loved one is 60+ and on a limited income.

localEntities.name: County social services agencies

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 60+ and struggling with grocery costs, CalFresh provides monthly funds loaded onto an EBT card for food purchases. Benefits range from a minimum of $25/month up to $306/month for individuals (from October 1, 2026), depending on income and expenses like medical costs and housing.

Because seniors get special eligibility rules, your loved one may qualify even if the full household wouldn't. Seniors can form their own separate household for CalFresh purposes, use net income after medical and housing deductions, and face no asset limits in most cases. The program also covers prepared meals at participating restaurants statewide through the Restaurant Meals Program.

SSI/SSP recipients can receive CalFresh in addition to their cash benefits, but they are not automatically income-eligible, they must apply and meet the same income rules as everyone else. Your loved one won't face work requirements, and all out-of-pocket medical expenses over $35 count as deductions to lower their countable income.

The $25 minimum is the federal floor and applies only to eligible one- and two-person households. Actual benefit depends on household size and the benefit calculation.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep CalFresh if they live in assisted living?
faqs.answer: Yes, residents of assisted living facilities can receive CalFresh benefits. However, if the facility provides all meals as part of the monthly fee, benefits may be reduced to the minimum $25/month. Your loved one can use benefits at grocery stores for snacks and additional food items.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is mostly Social Security, do they still qualify?
faqs.answer: Social Security counts as income, but seniors get special deductions for medical expenses over $35/month and housing costs. After these deductions, many seniors on Social Security still qualify. SSI/SSP recipients can receive CalFresh in addition to their cash benefits, though they still complete an application and are subject to the same income rules.

faqs.question: Can I apply for CalFresh on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, adult children can apply as an authorized representative for elderly or disabled parents. You'll need to complete a separate form designating you as their representative during the application process.

faqs.question: Does my loved one's house count against the asset limit?
faqs.answer: For most seniors, no. CalFresh in California generally does not apply an asset test, unlike Medi-Cal (which brought back asset limits in 2026), it looks at income rather than savings for the vast majority of households. In the rare case a household is subject to an asset review, the limit from October 1, 2026 is $4,750 when the household includes someone 60 or older, and the primary home, one vehicle, household goods, and retirement accounts are all excluded.

faqs.question: Can my loved one use CalFresh benefits at restaurants?
faqs.answer: Yes, through California's Restaurant Meals Program, seniors 60+ can use their EBT card to buy prepared meals at participating restaurants statewide. This is especially helpful for seniors who have difficulty cooking.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's medical expenses change during the year?
faqs.answer: Report increases in medical expenses to your county office immediately, this can increase monthly benefits. You must report changes within 10 days, and the county will recalculate benefits based on the new expenses.

faqs.question: Should my loved one apply as part of our family household or separately?
faqs.answer: Often separately. A senior can be treated as their own CalFresh household when they purchase and prepare their meals separately from others in the home, this is based on their meal situation, not a voluntary choice. Qualifying as a separate household often results in higher benefits.

faqs.question: How long do CalFresh benefits last once approved?
faqs.answer: Benefits continue as long as your loved one remains eligible. Seniors typically have longer certification periods (up to 24 months) before needing to reapply, compared to 12 months for younger adults. You'll receive renewal notices before benefits expire.

programs.name: LIHEAP (Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program)
programs.tagline: Help paying your loved one's heating and cooling bills if they're on a fixed income.

localEntities.name: Local LIHEAP service providers (find yours on CSD's Find Services In Your Area page)

programs.intro:
If your loved one's monthly income is below $3,332 (for a single person) or $4,357 (for a couple), LIHEAP can help pay their energy bills directly to the utility company. The program prioritizes households with high energy costs, elderly residents, people with disabilities, and families with young children.

Because federal funding is limited, even eligible households may not receive benefits. Priority goes to the most vulnerable, homes with medical equipment that requires electricity, elderly individuals facing shut-off notices, and households where energy costs consume a large portion of monthly income. Your loved one must continue paying their bills during the several-week application review process.

faqs.question: Can I apply if my loved one's name isn't on the utility bill?
faqs.answer: Yes. In many cases, any adult living in the household may apply for LIHEAP, even if they are not the utility account holder. If the utility account is in another person's name, an Account Holder Authorization and Consent Form may be required.

faqs.question: What if my loved one is already receiving SNAP or SSI?
faqs.answer: Households receiving SNAP, SSI, TANF, or certain veterans benefits may have a simpler income verification process or may already meet some eligibility requirements. However, an application is still required and approval is not automatic.

faqs.question: How much will LIHEAP actually pay toward my loved one's bill?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP benefit amounts vary based on factors such as household income, household size, energy costs, funding availability, and energy burden. Households with greater need may receive higher assistance amounts.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one gets a shut-off notice while the application is being reviewed?
faqs.answer: Applicants are encouraged to continue making utility payments when possible during the review process, since LIHEAP assistance is not guaranteed while applications are pending. Contact the utility company immediately to ask about payment plans, shut-off protection, or low-income programs such as CARE or FERA.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for LIHEAP and weatherization assistance at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes. LIHEAP and weatherization assistance are separate programs that may both be available through the same local service provider.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is slightly over the limit but they still can't afford their energy bills?
faqs.answer: If your loved one does not qualify for LIHEAP, ask the utility company about programs such as CARE, FERA, or Medical Baseline, which may offer discounts or additional support for qualifying households.

faqs.question: Does my loved one's house value affect LIHEAP eligibility?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP eligibility is generally based on household income, household size, and energy-related need rather than home ownership status or property value.

faqs.question: How often can my loved one receive LIHEAP benefits?
faqs.answer: LIHEAP assistance is generally available once per program year, though availability and requirements may vary by local agency and funding levels.

If your loved one struggles with high energy bills or lives in a drafty, hard-to-heat home, California's Weatherization Assistance Program provides free home improvements to reduce energy costs. The program installs insulation, seals air leaks, repairs or replaces heating systems and water heaters, and makes other efficiency upgrades at no cost to qualified households.

Because the program prioritizes households with adults 60 and older, your loved one may move up the waitlist faster than younger applicants. Average households save over $400 per year on energy bills after weatherization, with homes staying warmer in winter and cooler in summer. Services are available once every 15 years through local community providers across California.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they rent their home?
faqs.answer: Yes, renters are eligible, but your loved one must get written permission from their landlord before any weatherization work can begin. The landlord must approve the specific modifications that will be made to the property.

faqs.question: What if my loved one received weatherization services before?
faqs.answer: Your loved one can receive weatherization services once every 15 years. Under California Department of Community Services and Development (CSD) rules, if a home was weatherized with these funds within the last 15 years, they must wait until that period passes before applying again.

faqs.question: How long is the waitlist really?
faqs.answer: Waitlists vary significantly by region and funding availability. However, households with adults 60 and older receive priority placement, which can reduce wait times compared to younger applicants.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one has an emergency utility shutoff notice?
faqs.answer: Weatherization is not an emergency program and cannot stop a shut-off in time. If your loved one has an active disconnection notice, contact LIHEAP's Energy Crisis Intervention Program (ECIP), which works to halt disconnections within 24–48 hours, while weatherization is scheduled separately as a longer-term home improvement.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: You can help your loved one apply. Otherwise, bring their ID and have them available during the application.

faqs.question: What exactly gets installed or repaired?
faqs.answer: Common improvements include installing insulation, sealing air leaks, repairing or replacing heating systems and water heaters, and duct sealing. The specific work depends on your loved one's home assessment and what will provide the most energy savings.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply for both WAP and LIHEAP energy assistance?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one can receive both weatherization services through WAP and monthly utility bill assistance through LIHEAP. These are separate programs that complement each other.

faqs.question: What if the assessment shows my loved one's home needs more work than the program covers?
faqs.answer: The program provides a partial list of services and not all improvements are guaranteed. The technician will prioritize the most cost-effective energy-saving measures within the program's scope and budget.

HICAP counselors explain Medicare Parts A, B, and D, help compare Medicare Advantage Plans and Medigap policies, and identify cost-saving programs your loved one might qualify for.

This is not a financial assistance program, HICAP counselors help your loved one navigate their options but don't pay medical bills or premiums directly. Because counselors are trained specifically on Medicare rules and cost-saving programs, your loved one gets expert guidance without sales pressure from insurance companies.

HICAP serves all 58 California counties through regional agencies. Your loved one is eligible if they are a Medicare beneficiary of any age or are soon to be eligible.

faqs.question: What if my loved one lives in a different part of California?
faqs.answer: HICAP is a statewide program that provides free counseling in all 58 California counties. faqs.question: Can I get counseling on behalf of my loved one?

faqs.question: Will HICAP try to sell my loved one insurance?

Each meal provides at least one-third of daily nutritional requirements following federal dietary guidelines, plus an informal safety check and connection to other services.

The program serves homebound seniors who are isolated by illness, disability, or limited mobility. There's no income requirement statewide, though voluntary contributions are welcomed. Your loved one's spouse (any age) or a disabled household member may also receive meals if it benefits your loved one.

Meals on Wheels operates through 33 local Area Agencies on Aging across California, so availability, delivery schedules, and additional services vary by location. Some areas also offer to-go meal pickup options.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one lives outside the delivery zone?
faqs.answer: Local providers and Area Agencies on Aging serve designated counties or service areas. If your loved one lives outside the zone, ask about to-go meal pickup options or congregate meal sites. The AAA can also refer you to neighboring agencies that might serve your area.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one?

faqs.question: How much do families typically contribute for meals?

faqs.question: What if my loved one's health improves and they no longer need delivery?
faqs.answer: Contact your local provider to update your loved one's status. Many programs offer congregate meal options at senior centers as a transition, allowing your loved one to maintain nutrition support while socializing with others. Reassessment can happen anytime circumstances change.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get both Meals on Wheels and CalFresh benefits?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one can receive both programs simultaneously since Meals on Wheels provides prepared meals while CalFresh provides money for groceries. The combination can significantly improve nutrition security for homebound seniors with limited cooking ability.

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 55+ and unemployed with limited income, SCSEP is more than a paycheck, it's a way to stay active and connected, earning a stable income while training in friendly local settings like libraries, schools, and senior centers. Because participants work in community service roles at nonprofits and government agencies, your loved one earns income while gaining experience that makes them more employable. The program targets low-income seniors earning no more than 125% of the federal poverty level.

Your loved one will receive on-the-job training in computer or vocational skills plus professional job placement assistance to find permanent employment. Because SCSEP is designed as a bridge to regular employment, participants must remain unemployed throughout the program but receive dedicated support to transition to unsubsidized work. Hours vary by region, Orange County offers 16-29 hours per week depending on available funding.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's income increases during the program?
faqs.answer: Income must remain at or below 125% of the federal poverty level throughout participation. If your loved one's household income increases above this threshold, they may become ineligible and need to leave the program.

faqs.question: How long can my loved one stay in SCSEP?
faqs.answer: SCSEP is designed as temporary training, not permanent employment. The program focuses on building skills and experience to help participants transition to unsubsidized employment. Length of participation varies by individual progress and local provider policies.

faqs.question: What if there's no SCSEP provider in our county?

faqs.question: Will SCSEP income affect my loved one's other benefits?

faqs.question: What kind of work will my loved one do in SCSEP?
faqs.answer: Participants work at community service sites like nonprofits, schools, libraries, and government agencies. Jobs vary but often include clerical work, maintenance, childcare assistance, or community outreach. The goal is to build transferable job skills.

faqs.question: Does being a veteran really help with SCSEP enrollment?

faqs.question: Can I apply to multiple SCSEP providers at once?

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is slightly above the limit for their legal issue?
faqs.answer: Income guidelines can vary depending on the county, legal issue, and local provider. Some programs prioritize low-income seniors, while certain health-related or elder rights matters may have more flexible eligibility rules. Even if your loved one's income is slightly above a guideline, it's still worth calling to ask about available services or referrals.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my elderly loved one who can't travel?
faqs.answer: Yes. Many Senior Legal Services programs can speak with family members or caregivers and may offer phone appointments, outreach clinics, or accommodations for seniors with mobility or transportation challenges. Be sure to explain your loved one's situation when you call.

faqs.question: How do I find the right contact since this isn't one central program?
faqs.answer: California's senior legal services are coordinated through local Area Agencies on Aging and regional legal providers. programs.name: Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program
programs.tagline: Free advocacy when your loved one faces problems with nursing home or assisted living care quality, safety, or rights.

programs.intro:
If your loved one lives in a California nursing home, assisted living facility, or residential care home, they have access to free advocacy services when problems arise with care quality, safety, or their rights as a resident. The Long-Term Care Ombudsman Program provides independent advocates who investigate complaints, mediate conflicts with facility staff, and ensure your loved one's voice is heard in care decisions.

This is not a financial assistance program, ombudsman representatives are trained advocates who work directly with residents and facilities to resolve issues like inadequate care, billing disputes, unsafe conditions, or violations of resident rights. The program serves more than 8,000 long-term care facilities in California through 35 local Ombudsman programs.

Importantly, ombudsman representatives advocate for what your loved one wants, not necessarily what family members prefer. If there's disagreement between you and your loved one about care decisions, the ombudsman will support your loved one's expressed wishes.

faqs.question: Can I call the ombudsman about my loved one's facility even if my loved one doesn't want me to get involved?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can make the initial complaint, but the ombudsman will work according to your loved one's expressed wishes, not yours. If your loved one doesn't want advocacy services or disagrees with your concerns, the ombudsman will respect their decision and may not be able to take action you want them to take.

faqs.question: What's the difference between calling the ombudsman versus reporting to Adult Protective Services?
faqs.answer: In California, APS generally investigates abuse in private homes or community settings. If abuse or neglect happens inside a licensed facility, the Ombudsman and the state licensing agencies (Department of Public Health or Department of Social Services) are the primary investigators. For immediate life-threatening emergencies, always call 911 first. For care quality issues, rights violations, or non-emergency abuse concerns in a facility, start with the ombudsman.

faqs.question: Will the facility retaliate against my loved one if I file a complaint with the ombudsman?
faqs.answer: Retaliation against residents for ombudsman complaints is illegal under federal and state law. Ombudsman representatives are trained to monitor for retaliation and can take action if it occurs. However, you can request that complaints be handled confidentially when possible.

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 65+, disabled, or blind and receives federal SSI (Supplemental Security Income), California automatically provides an additional cash payment called State Supplementary Payment (SSP). This means your loved one gets more money each month, up to $239.94 extra for an individual or $607.83 extra for couples in 2026.

The total monthly payment becomes $1,233.94 for individuals or $2,098.83 for couples when combining federal SSI and California's SSP supplement. Because SSP follows SSI eligibility automatically, your loved one doesn't need to apply separately, if they qualify for SSI, they get SSP.

To qualify, your loved one must have very limited income (generally under $1,233.94/month after disregards) and assets under $2,000 for individuals or $3,000 for couples. The payment is reduced dollar-for-dollar by other countable income, and living arrangements can affect the amount.

faqs.question: Can my loved one keep their house if it's worth more than $2,000?
faqs.answer: Yes, your loved one's primary residence doesn't count toward the $2,000 asset limit regardless of value. Only cash, bank accounts, stocks, and other investments count as countable assets. The home remains exempt as long as your loved one lives in it.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one lives with me and I pay for their food?
faqs.answer: Free food and shelter count as in-kind income and will reduce your loved one's SSP payment. SSA calculates a dollar value for this support and deducts it from the monthly benefit amount. Keep records of any rent or food costs your loved one does pay.

faqs.question: Can I apply for SSI and SSP on behalf of my elderly loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, you can help your loved one apply or become their representative payee if SSA determines they can't manage their benefits. Call 1-800-772-1213 to discuss becoming an authorized representative during the application process.

faqs.question: Why hasn't my loved one's SSP amount increased with cost of living?
faqs.answer: California's SSP supplement hasn't received annual cost-of-living adjustments since cuts made in 2009-2011. While federal SSI gets annual increases, the state portion remains fixed, meaning SSP benefits have lost purchasing power to inflation over time.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income changes after they're approved?
faqs.answer: Report income changes to SSA immediately at 1-800-772-1213. SSP payments are reduced dollar-for-dollar by other countable income, so new income will decrease the monthly payment amount. SSA conducts periodic reviews to verify continued eligibility.

faqs.question: Can my loved one receive SSP if they move to another state?
faqs.answer: No, SSP is only for California residents. If your loved one moves to another state, they'll lose the California supplement but may qualify for that state's supplemental payment if one exists. They must report address changes to SSA immediately.

programs.name: Property Tax Postponement Program
programs.tagline: Defer your loved one's property taxes if they're 62+ on fixed income, taxes postponed with 7% interest until the home is sold.

localEntities.name: Administered centrally by California State Controller's Office

programs.intro:
If your loved one is 62+ and struggling to pay property taxes on their home, California can postpone the entire bill until they sell or move. This program defers current-year property taxes with 7% annual interest, creating immediate cash flow relief for seniors on fixed income.

Your loved one must have household income of $55,181 or less and own at least 40% equity in their home. The postponed taxes become a lien on the property, repaid when the home is sold, transferred, or after death. Because this affects your family's inheritance, discuss the long-term financial impact before applying.

Funding is limited and distributed first-come, first-served during the annual application period (typically October through February). Your loved one must reapply every year to confirm continued eligibility.

faqs.question: What happens to the postponed taxes when my loved one dies or we sell the house?
faqs.answer: The postponed taxes plus 7% annual interest become due immediately upon sale, transfer, death, or when your loved one stops living in the home as their primary residence. The state holds a lien on the property that must be paid from the sale proceeds or estate.

faqs.question: Can my loved one apply if they co-own the house with someone under 62?
faqs.answer: All recorded property owners must be 62+, blind, or disabled, except for spouses, registered domestic partners, and direct-line relatives (children, grandchildren, or their spouses). If other co-owners don't meet these criteria, your loved one won't qualify.

faqs.question: How much equity does my loved one need in their home to qualify?
faqs.answer: Your loved one must own at least 40% equity, meaning total mortgages, liens, and other encumbrances cannot exceed 60% of the property's fair market value. Any existing delinquent taxes count toward encumbrances and reduce available equity.

faqs.question: What if my loved one's income is slightly over $55,181?
faqs.answer: The income limit is firm at $55,181 for household income in the prior calendar year, regardless of household size. Income includes all household members except minors, full-time students, and renters. If income exceeds this limit, your loved one cannot qualify.

faqs.question: Can my loved one postpone taxes if they already have a reverse mortgage?
faqs.answer: No, properties with reverse mortgages are not eligible for the Property Tax Postponement Program. This is a firm program requirement with no exceptions.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one misses the annual application deadline?
faqs.answer: Your loved one must wait until the next application period to apply. The program only accepts applications during specific months each year (typically October through February), and late applications are not accepted.

programs.name: In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS)
programs.tagline: If your loved one needs daily help at home to stay safe, IHSS provides up to 283 hours per month of personal care and housework support.

localEntities.name: County IHSS offices (find via https://www.cdss.ca.gov/in-home-supportive-services or county social services)

programs.intro:
If your loved one is on Medi-Cal and needs daily help with bathing, meal preparation, or housework but wants to stay in their own home, IHSS provides in-home care services up to 283 hours per month. Because IHSS covers personal care, housecleaning, grocery shopping, and even accompaniment to medical appointments, your loved one can avoid nursing home placement while getting the support they need.

Your loved one must be eligible for Medi-Cal first, either through SSI/SSP or by meeting income limits of $1,836/month for a single person (effective April 1, 2026). Because services are based on a county assessment of functional need, the hours authorized depend on your loved one's specific limitations with daily activities like dressing, grooming, or medication management.

The program requires a physician to complete a Health Care Certification form (SOC 873) confirming your loved one needs assistance, and a county social worker conducts a home assessment to determine service hours. Your loved one must live in their own home or chosen residence, nursing homes and licensed care facilities don't qualify.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get IHSS if they don't have Medi-Cal yet?
faqs.answer: No, Medi-Cal eligibility is required before IHSS services begin. However, you can apply for both programs at the same time. SSI/SSP recipients automatically qualify, while others must meet income limits of $1,836/month for singles or $2,490/month for couples (effective April 1, 2026).

faqs.question: What if my loved one's house is worth more than the asset limit?
faqs.answer: The primary residence is exempt from asset limits, meaning your loved one can keep their home regardless of value. For 2026, other countable assets (like secondary property or investments) must stay below $130,000 for individuals or $195,000 for couples.

faqs.question: Can a family member be paid to provide IHSS services?
faqs.answer: Yes, in most cases family members can be hired as IHSS providers and receive payment for authorized hours. Spouses cannot be providers in most situations, but adult children, relatives, and friends can typically be hired through the program.

faqs.question: How many hours will my loved one actually get?
faqs.answer: Authorized hours depend on a county assessment of functional limitations. The maximum is 283 hours per month. The average recipient in 2026 is authorized for approximately 127 hours per month.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's condition gets worse after enrollment?
faqs.answer: You can request a reassessment if your loved one's functional needs increase. Contact your county IHSS office to schedule a new evaluation, which may result in additional authorized hours if the assessment shows greater need for assistance.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get IHSS while living in assisted living?
faqs.answer: No, IHSS is only available for people living in their own homes or chosen residences. Licensed care facilities, nursing homes, and assisted living facilities don't qualify because they already provide supervised care.

faqs.question: How long does the county assessment take?
faqs.answer: The home visit typically takes 1–3 hours. The social worker will observe your loved one's ability to perform daily tasks and review the required SOC 873 medical form.

faqs.question: What if the county denies our application?
faqs.answer: You have the right to appeal any denial or reduction in services. The county must provide written reasons for denial, and you can request a fair hearing through the California Department of Social Services within 90 days of the notice.

faqs.question: Can I use CRC services if I'm already getting IHSS for my loved one?
faqs.answer: Yes, CRC services complement IHSS. While IHSS provides paid caregiving hours, CRC offers counseling, support groups, legal consultation, and additional respite funding that IHSS doesn't cover. You can use both programs simultaneously.

faqs.question: What if I live near a county border, which CRC do I use?

faqs.question: Do I need my loved one's permission to get CRC services?

faqs.question: Can multiple family members get CRC services for the same parent?
faqs.answer: Yes, if multiple family members are providing unpaid care, each caregiver can access services independently. This is common when siblings share caregiving responsibilities and each needs different types of support.

faqs.question: Can my loved one get CBAS if they live in a rural area without a nearby center?
faqs.answer: No. Your loved one must live within one hour's drive of a CBAS center. Only 28 of California's 58 counties have certified centers. If there's no center within an hour, your loved one cannot access CBAS services, but they may qualify for other programs like IHSS or MSSP.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's assets are just over the new $130,000 limit?
faqs.answer: They won't qualify for CBAS as of January 1, 2026. The primary residence and one vehicle don't count toward the limit, but all other assets do. Consider consulting an elder law attorney about legal spend-down strategies if they're close to the limit.

faqs.question: Can I apply for CBAS if my loved one has Medicare but not Medi-Cal?
faqs.answer: No. CBAS is exclusively a Medi-Cal benefit. Your loved one must first qualify for and enroll in Medi-Cal. However, Adult Day Health Care (ADHC) remains available for private-pay participants who don't have Medi-Cal.

faqs.question: How many days per week will my loved one actually receive services?
faqs.answer: Services can be approved up to 7 days per week, but the specific frequency depends on your loved one's individual needs assessment and your Managed Care Plan's approval. Program materials don't specify standard service hours or typical approval patterns.

faqs.question: What if my loved one has mild dementia but can still do most daily activities independently?
faqs.answer: A dementia diagnosis alone doesn't guarantee eligibility. Your loved one must demonstrate functional impairment through the CBAS Eligibility Determination Tool (CEDT) assessment. Mild cognitive impairment and moderate Alzheimer's (stage 4 dementia) are qualifying diagnoses, but functional need must still be proven.

faqs.question: Can I choose which CBAS center my loved one attends?
faqs.answer: You can select from available certified centers within your area, but your choices are limited to the 310 centers across 28 counties. Your Managed Care Plan will help identify nearby options after approval, and availability may vary by center.

faqs.question: What happens if my loved one's condition improves and they no longer need daily help?
faqs.answer: CBAS eligibility requires ongoing functional impairment. If your loved one's condition significantly improves, they would need reassessment and might no longer qualify. However, program materials don't specify reassessment frequency or procedures for condition changes.

faqs.question: Can my loved one be on a waiting list for a nursing home and still get CBAS?
faqs.answer: Yes. CBAS is designed as an alternative to nursing home care for people who can live at home with appropriate support services. Being on a nursing home waiting list doesn't disqualify someone from CBAS, and the program may help delay or prevent nursing home placement.

programs.name: Medi-Cal for Aged and Disabled
programs.tagline: If your parent is 65 or older and living on a fixed income in California, they may qualify for full medical coverage with no monthly premium and no out-of-pocket share of cost.

programs.intro:
If your parent is 65 or older (or under 65 and disabled) and their monthly income falls below $1,836 for a single person, they may qualify for Medi-Cal for Aged and Disabled. This is full-scope Medi-Cal coverage with zero share of cost, meaning no monthly premiums, no copays, and no deductibles. It covers doctor visits, hospital stays, prescription drugs, ambulance transport, and home care services.

This is not a supplemental plan layered on top of another insurance. For many older Californians with low income, it is their primary or only health coverage. Because there is no share of cost under the Aged and Disabled Federal Poverty Level (A&D FPL) category, your parent pays nothing for covered medical services. That can mean thousands of dollars a year in avoided costs for someone managing chronic conditions or multiple medications.

Two tests apply: income and assets. Meeting the income limit alone is not enough. A single person must also have countable assets of $130,000 or less (the primary home and one vehicle are not counted). If your parent is not yet receiving Social Security disability benefits and disability is the basis for eligibility rather than age, the county may need additional time to verify that status, which can extend processing beyond the standard 45 days.

steps.description: Pull together your parent's Social Security award letter, a document showing California residency (utility bill or lease), and proof of income. If disability rather than age is the basis for the application, gather any SSA disability determination letters or medical records you have. Having these ready prevents the most common processing delay.

steps.title: Apply online through BenefitsCal
steps.description: Go to BenefitsCal at benefitscal.com and complete the Single Streamlined Application. The system screens for Medi-Cal eligibility automatically. You can also start at the DHCS application page at dhcs.ca.gov/medi-cal/apply/ for links to county portals and additional guidance. If you prefer to apply through Covered California (coveredca.gov), that application also routes to Medi-Cal automatically when the applicant appears eligible.

steps.title: Or apply by phone, mail, or in person
steps.description: If online is not workable, call your county Medi-Cal office to request a paper application. You can mail the completed application back to the county, or bring it in person to the local county social services or Medi-Cal office. Processing timelines are the same regardless of how you apply.

steps.title: Respond to any county requests quickly
steps.description: After submission, the county may send a notice requesting additional documents or scheduling an interview. Respond as quickly as possible. Missing a document request is the most common reason applications stall. If disability must be established, the county may take up to 90 days rather than the standard 45.

steps.title: Receive your eligibility determination
steps.description: The county will mail a notice of decision. If approved, coverage can be retroactive to the month of application in some cases. If denied, the notice will include appeal rights and deadlines. You have the right to request a state fair hearing if you disagree with the decision.

applicationGuide.tip: If your parent already receives SSI (Supplemental Security Income), they are typically automatically eligible for Medi-Cal and may not need to file a separate application. Check with the county office to confirm enrollment status.

These are related but not identical to the A&D FPL category described here. Ask the county specifically about both options.

If your parent is in the hospital or a rehabilitation facility right now, you can apply while they are still there. Hospital discharge planners and social workers can often help initiate the application or provide documentation. Do not wait until discharge.

contentSections.title: What zero share of cost actually means
contentSections.body: Under the A&D FPL category, your parent pays nothing for covered Medi-Cal services. No copays at the doctor. No cost-sharing for hospital stays. No deductible for prescriptions. This is different from the Medi-Cal share-of-cost category, where enrollees must spend a set amount on medical bills each month before Medi-Cal activates. Make sure the county is evaluating your parent for the A&D FPL category specifically, not defaulting to a share-of-cost pathway.

contentSections.title: The asset test: what counts and what does not
contentSections.body: Your parent's home does not count toward the $130,000 asset limit, regardless of what it is worth. One vehicle does not count. What does count: bank account balances, CDs, stocks, bonds, investment accounts, and the cash value of life insurance policies above certain thresholds. If your parent has savings or investments approaching $130,000, verify with the county exactly how each account is classified before assuming they are ineligible. The rules around which assets are countable can be more nuanced than a simple list suggests.

contentSections.title: Income and assets are two separate tests
contentSections.body: Passing the income test does not mean your parent automatically passes the asset test, and vice versa. Both must be met. A common situation: a parent with very low monthly Social Security income who has accumulated savings over $130,000 would not qualify under the A&D FPL category as described in county guidance, even though their monthly income is well below the limit. If assets are the obstacle, ask the county about any spend-down or asset-restructuring options that may be permissible.

faqs.question: My parent's monthly income is $1,900, just above the single-person limit. Are they completely out of options?
faqs.answer: Not necessarily. The A&D FPL category described here has a $1,836/month limit for a single person. But California Medi-Cal has other pathways for aged and disabled individuals whose income is somewhat higher, including a share-of-cost category where Medi-Cal activates after your parent spends a set amount on medical bills each month. Ask the county specifically about all available Medi-Cal categories for aged and disabled applicants, not just the A&D FPL path.

faqs.question: My parent owns their home. Does the home value count against the $130,000 asset limit?
faqs.answer: No. The primary home is exempt from the asset calculation for the A&D FPL Medi-Cal category. It does not matter what the home is worth. One vehicle is also exempt. The asset limit applies to countable resources such as bank accounts, savings, CDs, investments, and similar holdings.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent if they cannot manage the paperwork themselves?
faqs.answer: Yes. You can apply as an authorized representative on your parent's behalf. You will need to indicate this on the application and may be asked to provide documentation of your authority to act, such as a power of attorney. The county Medi-Cal office can walk you through what they require. Call your county office or use BenefitsCal at benefitscal.com to start the process.

faqs.question: My parent is not receiving Social Security disability benefits yet but may qualify based on a medical condition. Can they still apply for this program?
faqs.answer: Yes, but the process takes longer. If SSA has not yet made a disability determination, the county must make its own disability evaluation. This can extend the processing window from the standard 45 days to up to 90 days. Submit all available medical documentation with the initial application to reduce back-and-forth delays. Once SSA issues a disability determination, that determination can be used to establish eligibility going forward.

faqs.question: If my parent qualifies for Medi-Cal for Aged and Disabled and also has Medicare, how do the two programs interact?
faqs.answer: When someone qualifies for both Medicare and Medi-Cal, they are considered dually eligible. In that situation, Medicare generally pays first for covered services, and Medi-Cal may cover costs that Medicare does not, such as copays, deductibles, or services Medicare does not include. Your parent may also be eligible for a Medicare Savings Program, which has Medi-Cal help pay Medicare premiums. Ask the county about both at the same time when you apply.

faqs.question: My parent lives in a skilled nursing facility. Can they still get Medi-Cal for Aged and Disabled?
faqs.answer: The A&D FPL category described here is generally for individuals who do not reside in a long-term care facility. If your parent is in a nursing home, a different Medi-Cal category applies with different income and asset rules. Contact the county Medi-Cal office directly to discuss the correct pathway. The facility's social worker or discharge planner can also help initiate the right type of application.

faqs.question: What happens if my parent's income or assets change after they are enrolled?
faqs.answer: Enrollees are required to report changes in income, assets, or household circumstances to the county. Medi-Cal eligibility is redetermined periodically, typically annually. If income or assets rise above the applicable limits, eligibility may end or shift to a different Medi-Cal category such as share-of-cost. Report changes to your county Medi-Cal office as they occur rather than waiting for the annual renewal.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for Medi-Cal for Aged and Disabled and In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS) at the same time?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it often makes sense to do both. IHSS pays for in-home care for Medi-Cal-eligible adults who need help with daily activities like bathing, dressing, and medication management. Medi-Cal eligibility is a requirement for IHSS, so applying for both simultaneously means IHSS processing can begin once Medi-Cal is approved. Ask the county about initiating both applications together through BenefitsCal or at the county social services office.

programs.name: California Assisted Living Waiver (ALW)
programs.tagline: If your parent needs nursing-home-level care but wants to stay in assisted living instead, Medi-Cal may pay for their care services through this waiver so they never have to enter a facility.

programs.intro:
If your parent qualifies for a nursing facility but you want them to live in assisted living instead, the California Assisted Living Waiver pays for the personal care, homemaker, and coordination services that make that possible. Medi-Cal covers the care services; your parent still pays room and board, usually from SSI/SSP or personal funds.

The program is only available in 15 counties: Alameda, Contra Costa, Fresno, Kern, Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, Sacramento, San Bernardino, San Diego, San Francisco, San Joaquin, San Mateo, Santa Clara, and Sonoma. Your parent must already have full-scope Medi-Cal with zero share of cost. If Medi-Cal has assigned them a share of cost, they are not eligible for ALW even if they otherwise qualify.

The most important thing to understand: this is not a cash benefit and it does not pay rent. It pays for the services your parent needs to live safely in an assisted living setting rather than a nursing home. Getting in requires a clinical level-of-care assessment, a participating ALW provider in your county, and Medi-Cal enrollment without a share of cost. All three gates must open before enrollment can begin.

The facility itself must be ALW-qualified; not every licensed assisted living facility participates.

steps.title: Contact the provider or care coordination agency to initiate enrollment
steps.description: The participating provider or care coordination agency guides the enrollment process. They will request your parent's Medi-Cal information, initiate the nursing-facility level-of-care assessment, and submit the required ALW enrollment paperwork including the ALW Program Application Checklist.

steps.title: Complete the level-of-care assessment
steps.description: A clinical reviewer assesses whether your parent meets Nursing Facility Level of Care. This assessment reviews daily functioning, medical needs, and care requirements. Your parent must pass this review to proceed.

steps.title: Confirm room and board funding
steps.description: ALW pays for care services only. Your parent must have a way to pay rent and meals at the facility, most commonly through SSI/SSP benefits or personal funds. Confirm this with the facility before finalizing placement.

applicationGuide.waitlist: Access can be constrained by local provider availability and county enrollment capacity. No official statewide waitlist length is published. Ask the specific provider or care coordination agency about current wait times in your county when you make contact.

If your county has no current ALW provider openings, ask the care coordination agency about other Medi-Cal Home and Community-Based Services (HCBS) options such as IHSS or PACE, which may serve your parent in the meantime.

contentSections.title: What ALW pays for and what it does not
contentSections.body:
ALW covers: personal care (bathing, dressing, grooming), homemaker services, home health aide services, care coordination, residential habilitation, and nursing facility transition support.

ALW does not cover: room and board (rent and meals at the facility). Your parent must pay those costs separately, typically using SSI/SSP benefits or personal funds. This is one of the most common sources of confusion when families start the process.

contentSections.title: Two types of ALW settings
contentSections.body: ALW services can be delivered in two settings. The first is a licensed Residential Care Facility for the Elderly (RCFE) or Adult Residential Facility (ARF), which is the traditional assisted living model. The second is publicly subsidized senior or disabled housing, where the same services are delivered under the name Assisted Care rather than Assisted Living Services. The clinical eligibility requirements and Medi-Cal rules are the same in both settings. Which type is available depends on your county and local provider participation.

faqs.question: My parent has a Medi-Cal share of cost. Can they still apply for ALW?
faqs.answer: No. A Medi-Cal share of cost disqualifies a person from ALW enrollment entirely, even if they meet every other requirement. Your parent must have full-scope Medi-Cal with zero share of cost before they can enroll. Contact your parent's county Medi-Cal office to find out whether the share of cost can be reduced or eliminated, or ask about spend-down pathways.

faqs.question: Does ALW pay for my parent's room and board at the assisted living facility?
faqs.answer: No. ALW pays only for care services: personal care, homemaker tasks, home health aide support, and care coordination. Your parent must independently cover rent and meals at the facility. Most participants use SSI/SSP benefits for this. Confirm with the specific facility what the monthly room and board cost is before committing.

faqs.question: How do I know if the assisted living facility we are considering actually participates in ALW?
faqs.answer: Not every licensed RCFE or ARF participates. The facility must be enrolled as an ALW provider with DHCS. Before touring or signing any agreement, ask the facility directly whether it holds an active ALW provider agreement. You can also check the DHCS ALW program page at dhcs.ca.gov/services/long-term-care-alternatives-home-and-community-based-service-options/assisted-living-waiver/ for guidance on finding participating providers.

faqs.question: My parent's county is not on the ALW list. Are there alternatives?
faqs.answer: Yes. If your parent's county is not among the 15 ALW counties, three Medi-Cal programs worth exploring are In-Home Supportive Services (IHSS), which funds personal care at home; PACE (Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly), which provides all-inclusive care for people who qualify for nursing-home level care; and Community-Based Adult Services (CBAS), which provides day-program support. Each has its own eligibility rules.

faqs.question: What is the nursing-facility level of care assessment and who conducts it?
faqs.answer: It is a clinical review that determines whether your parent's functional and medical needs are severe enough to require the level of care provided in a nursing home. The assessment typically examines how much help your parent needs with daily activities like bathing, dressing, eating, mobility, and medication management. The participating ALW provider or care coordination agency arranges this assessment as part of the enrollment process. Your parent must pass this review to qualify.

faqs.question: Can I apply for ALW while my parent is still in a nursing facility?
faqs.answer: Yes, and this is one of the intended use cases. ALW includes a specific benefit called Nursing Facility Transition Care Coordination to help people move from a nursing facility back into the community. Tell the care coordination agency upfront that your parent is currently in a nursing facility and wants to transition to assisted living. Discharge planners at the facility may also be able to help initiate the process.

faqs.question: How long will it take to get my parent enrolled?
faqs.answer: DHCS does not publish a statewide processing timeline. Enrollment depends on confirming Medi-Cal eligibility, completing the level-of-care assessment, finding an ALW-participating facility with an opening, and county-level capacity. In practice, the biggest variable is local provider availability. Ask the specific care coordination agency or facility about current wait times in your county when you first make contact.

faqs.question: Can my parent apply for both ALW and IHSS at the same time?
faqs.answer: These programs serve different living situations. IHSS pays for in-home care when a person lives in their own home. ALW pays for care services when a person lives in a participating assisted living facility. A person generally cannot receive both simultaneously for the same care needs. If your parent is currently at home using IHSS and is considering a move to assisted living, ask a care coordination agency how the transition would affect their existing IHSS services.

programs.name: California PACE Programs
programs.tagline: If your parent is 55+ and needs nursing-home-level care but wants to stay home, PACE covers almost everything: doctors, medications, home care, meals, and transportation, all under one coordinated team.

localEntities.name: Local PACE organizations and PACE centers in participating California service areas

programs.intro:
PACE (Program of All-Inclusive Care for the Elderly) is for people 55 and older who need a nursing-home level of care but can still live at home safely with support. If your parent qualifies, one PACE team takes over all their medical and long-term care: primary care, specialists, medications, physical therapy, home care, dental, vision, hearing, mental health, meals, and transportation to appointments. You do not coordinate between providers because the PACE team does that.

For people who have both Medicare and Medi-Cal, PACE typically costs nothing out of pocket. People who have only Medicare or only Medi-Cal may pay a partial premium, and people without either can enroll by paying privately. There is no income or asset test to qualify; eligibility is based on age, where your parent lives, and whether a clinical assessment confirms they need nursing-home-level care.

PACE is not available everywhere in California. Each PACE organization serves specific counties and zip codes, and the enrollment process runs through that local organization rather than a statewide office. Your first step is confirming whether a PACE plan operates in your parent's zip code.

steps.title: Confirm your parent's zip code is in a PACE service area
steps.description: Go to the California DHCS PACE page at dhcs.ca.gov and use the list of participating PACE organizations to find one that covers your parent's county and zip code. If none appears for your area, PACE is not currently available there.

steps.title: Contact the local PACE organization
steps.description: Call or go online to the specific PACE organization serving your parent's area. Each organization runs its own enrollment office. Ask to speak with an enrollment coordinator. They will screen for basic eligibility (age, zip code) on this first call.

steps.title: Complete the health assessment
steps.description: A PACE interdisciplinary team will conduct a clinical assessment of your parent's care needs to determine whether they meet the Nursing Facility Level of Care standard. This typically involves a home visit or in-person evaluation. Bring your parent's current medication list, recent medical records, and names of current doctors.

steps.title: Submit enrollment documents
steps.description: Provide proof of age, proof of residence in the service area, Medicare card if applicable, Medi-Cal card if applicable, and any insurance information. Each PACE organization handles its own paperwork; there is no single statewide enrollment form.

steps.title: Review and sign the enrollment agreement
steps.description: Once the assessment is complete and eligibility is confirmed, the PACE organization will present an enrollment agreement. Your parent (or their authorized representative) signs voluntarily. PACE covers care from the enrollment date forward.

applicationGuide.processingTime: The application and health assessment combined typically take a few weeks. The clinical assessment phase is the main variable.
applicationGuide.tip: If your parent is being discharged from a hospital or skilled nursing facility, ask the discharge planner whether PACE is available in their home zip code. Discharge planners often know local PACE contacts and can speed up the initial outreach.

applicationNotes: PACE eligibility hinges on the clinical assessment, not paperwork. The biggest reason families get stuck is not documents but the level-of-care determination. Come to the assessment with a clear picture of everything your parent needs help with daily, including things they may downplay.
Your parent must live inside a specific zip code served by the PACE organization, not just the county. Call before investing time in the enrollment process to confirm coverage at their exact address.
People who have only Medicare (no Medi-Cal) or who are paying privately can still enroll. Ask the PACE organization about premium amounts that apply to your parent's specific insurance situation.

Enrollment is voluntary and your parent can disenroll at any time. PACE is not a one-way door, and families sometimes worry unnecessarily about locking in. The decision can be revisited if circumstances change.

contentSections.title: PACE is not the same as PACE financing for home improvements
contentSections.body: California has two completely different programs that use the acronym PACE. The senior care program on this page coordinates medical care and long-term support. The other PACE (Property Assessed Clean Energy) finances solar panels and home energy upgrades. If someone directed you here for home improvement financing, that is a different program entirely.

contentSections.title: What PACE actually covers
contentSections.body: When your parent enrolls in PACE, a single interdisciplinary team becomes responsible for all of the following: primary care visits, specialist referrals, prescription medications, physical and occupational therapy, restorative therapy, skilled nursing care, home health aide visits, personal care (bathing, dressing, grooming), social work services, mental and behavioral health services, dental care, vision care, hearing care, nutritional counseling, meals, recreational therapy, durable medical equipment, and transportation to the PACE center and to medical appointments. Families often describe enrollment as the moment they stopped spending hours each week coordinating between providers.

contentSections.title: Cost: what your parent actually pays
contentSections.body: If your parent has both Medicare and Medi-Cal (dual eligible), PACE typically costs nothing out of pocket. The PACE organization is paid a set monthly amount by Medicare and Medi-Cal to cover all care. If your parent has only Medicare, a monthly premium for the Medi-Cal portion of services may apply; ask the local PACE organization for the current amount in your area. If your parent has neither, private-pay enrollment is available and the PACE organization can quote a monthly cost. No figures are published statewide because amounts vary by plan and individual coverage.

faqs.question: My parent has Medicare but not Medi-Cal. Can they still enroll in PACE?
faqs.answer: Yes. PACE does not require both Medicare and Medi-Cal. Your parent may enroll with Medicare only or even without either program by paying privately. If they have Medicare but not Medi-Cal, a monthly premium for the long-term care portion may apply. Contact the local PACE organization in your parent's zip code and ask specifically about the cost structure for Medicare-only enrollees.

faqs.question: My parent owns a home and has savings. Does that disqualify them?
faqs.answer: No. PACE has no income or asset limit. Eligibility is based on age (55+), living in a PACE service area, and meeting the Nursing Facility Level of Care clinical standard. Owning a home or having savings does not affect eligibility. PACE is a medical and care coordination program, not a means-tested financial benefit.

faqs.question: What does 'nursing-home level of care' actually mean for the assessment?
faqs.answer: It means a clinical team will evaluate whether your parent needs ongoing help with activities like bathing, dressing, mobility, medication management, or supervision for cognitive impairment at a level that would qualify them for nursing home admission under California standards. Meeting this standard does not mean your parent has to go to a nursing home; it is the clinical threshold that makes them eligible for PACE's comprehensive support at home.

faqs.question: Can I apply on behalf of my parent, or do they have to do it themselves?
faqs.answer: An authorized representative, including an adult child with a signed authorization or a legal power of attorney, can initiate the enrollment process and handle paperwork on your parent's behalf. However, PACE enrollment is voluntary, so your parent must be able to consent to joining the program. If your parent has a legal representative (guardian, conservator, or healthcare proxy), that person can consent in their place.

faqs.question: What if my parent's condition worsens after enrollment? Will PACE drop them?
faqs.answer: PACE is designed specifically for people whose needs increase over time. As your parent's condition changes, the interdisciplinary team adjusts the care plan, which can include more home care hours, skilled nursing visits, or short-term stays in a nursing facility covered by PACE. PACE does not discharge participants because their care needs increase. The only reason a person would leave PACE involuntarily is if they permanently move outside the service area or if they require 24-hour nursing care that PACE cannot safely arrange in a home setting.

faqs.question: Is PACE available everywhere in California?
faqs.answer: No. PACE operates only in specific counties and zip codes served by participating organizations. Availability depends on whether a PACE plan has been established in your parent's area and whether that plan has capacity. Go to the California DHCS PACE page at dhcs.ca.gov to find organizations serving your parent's location. If none serves their zip code, PACE is not currently an option, and you would need to look at alternatives like IHSS or CBAS.

faqs.question: Can my parent enroll in PACE and also keep seeing their current doctor?
faqs.answer: When your parent enrolls in PACE, the PACE interdisciplinary team becomes responsible for all of their medical care. In most cases, outside providers are no longer covered by Medicare or Medi-Cal because the PACE plan takes on that full responsibility. If your parent has a strong relationship with a specific specialist, ask the local PACE organization whether that provider participates or whether a referral arrangement is possible. This is one of the most important questions to ask before enrolling.

faqs.question: Can my parent disenroll from PACE if it is not working for them?
faqs.answer: Yes. PACE enrollment is always voluntary and your parent can disenroll at any time without penalty. Disenrollment typically takes effect the first of the following month. After leaving PACE, your parent's Medicare and Medi-Cal coverage returns to standard fee-for-service or their previous managed care plan. Ask the local PACE organization about transition planning before disenrolling so there is no gap in care.

stateOverview.intro: California offers 16 major programs to help seniors age in place, from covering Medicare costs to providing daily home care. If your loved one is 60+ and struggling with medical bills, grocery costs, or daily tasks, you likely qualify for multiple forms of help. California's programs range from cash assistance (up to $298/month for food through CalFresh) to comprehensive care coordination (MSSP can provide nursing oversight and personal care to keep your loved one out of a nursing home). Most programs have income limits around $1,700-2,200/month for single seniors, but several resources like HICAP counseling and legal services are free regardless of income. Start by checking the programs below that match your biggest concerns, many families qualify for 3-4 different types of assistance.

stateOverview.resourcesVsBenefits: California offers both income-qualified benefits and free resources for all seniors. Benefits like CalFresh, IHSS, and Medicare Savings Programs require income verification and provide direct financial assistance or services. Free resources like HICAP counseling, Caregiver Resource Centers, and California Senior Legal Services are available regardless of income, these help you navigate the system, understand your options, and solve problems without qualifying for specific dollar amounts.
